title: Cables and voltages
learned: Every cable carries a voltage; what it means depends on where it goes
Audio swings fast (you hear it), CV moves slowly (it turns knobs for you)
A gate is on or off: it says WHEN; V/OCT says HOW HIGH: 1 V = one octave
One output can feed many inputs; an input takes one cable

steps.why: In a modular synth everything runs on voltage. The sound itself is a fast-changing voltage, and a knob movement or a key press is sent on to other modules as a voltage too. Once you see that, patching starts to make sense.
steps.do: The rack is turned to the back. Press Next.

steps.why: Let's look at an audio signal first.
steps.do: Patch your first cable: press the left mouse button on the SAW socket of the oscillator, hold it, move to the IN 1 socket of the scope and let go. SAW is an output, IN 1 an input: a cable always goes from an output to an input.
steps.after: The scope draws the voltage over time: the first line (trace) is a sawtooth swinging between -5 V and +5 V hundreds of times a second. A voltage that moves this fast is audio: if it reached a speaker you would hear a tone.

steps.why: Now a slow voltage from the LFO (low-frequency oscillator).
steps.do: Drag a cable from SIN of the LFO to IN 2 of the scope.
steps.after: The second trace is almost a flat line that slowly rises and falls, about once a second: too slow to hear. Slow voltages are control voltages (CV): they do not sound, they move things, like a hand turning a knob.
steps.try: Turn to the front (F1) and turn RATE on the LFO: drag the knob up or down (or turn the wheel over it). Trace 2 moves faster. Then F2.

steps.why: Here is CV doing its job: the LFO will move the pitch of the oscillator.
steps.do: Add a second cable from SIN of the LFO to V/OCT of the oscillator. SIN already has a cable, and a plain drag from it would pick that cable up and move it. For a new one, hold Ctrl and drag from SIN to V/OCT. Or right-click SIN: the menu lists New cable in several colours; press the left mouse button on the colour you like, keep holding and drag to V/OCT.
steps.after: The waves of trace 1 now bunch together and spread out: the pitch goes up and down with the LFO. V/OCT means volts per octave: +1 V is one octave up, so the LFO's ±5 V sweeps five octaves up and five down. One output fed two inputs: an output can feed as many as you like.

steps.why: Taking a cable out is just as important as plugging one in.
steps.do: Remove the cable from the LFO to V/OCT: press the left mouse button on the V/OCT socket, drag the cable away and let go over an empty spot. (Shift+click on a socket also removes its top cable.)
steps.after: The pitch is steady again. An input takes only one cable; plugging a new one into a taken input replaces the old cable.

steps.why: The last kind is the gate: on or off, like a key that is held or let go. The envelope turns a gate into a shape.
steps.do: Drag a cable from ENV of the envelope to IN 2 of the scope (it replaces the LFO cable there), turn to the front (F1) and press and hold the PUSH button of the envelope for a moment.
steps.after: While you held PUSH, the envelope got a gate: it rose (attack), fell to a level (decay, sustain) and faded when you let go (release). Gates say WHEN, envelopes say HOW a note moves.

steps.do: Audio, CV, gates and pitch: all of them are voltages, each doing a different job. Press Next to finish.
